xss-reflected.what: Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) occurs when user input is immediately echoed back into a web page without proper sanitization or encoding. The malicious script is 'reflected' off the server in the response.
xss-reflected.why: Attackers can steal session cookies, perform actions as the victim, redirect to malicious sites, or deface web pages. This vulnerability allows complete control over what the victim sees and does on the website.

hints.title: Beginner Hint
hints.text: Try adding a simple <script> tag to the URL query parameter. Look at what gets reflected in the page.

hints.title: Intermediate Hint
hints.text: If

hints.title: Solution
hints.text: Payload: - This creates an image tag that triggers JavaScript when the image fails to load.

steps: Open your browser's Developer Tools (F12) and go to the Console tab

If that's blocked, try an event handler:
Observe the JavaScript alert() confirming successful XSS execution
Check the page source to see how your input was reflected unsafely

sqli-error.what: SQL Injection occurs when user input is directly concatenated into SQL queries without proper sanitization, allowing attackers to manipulate database queries.
sqli-error.why: Attackers can extract sensitive data, modify or delete database records, bypass authentication, or in some cases execute operating system commands. This is one of the most critical web vulnerabilities.

hints.title: Beginner Hint
hints.text: Try adding a single quote (') to the input field and observe the error message.

hints.title: Intermediate Hint
hints.text: Use SQL keywords like 'OR', 'UNION', or 'SELECT' to manipulate the query logic.

hints.title: Solution
hints.text: Payload: ' OR '1'='1 - This makes the WHERE clause always true, potentially returning all records.

fix.insecure: query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + userInput;

steps: Enter a single quote (') in the input field
Observe the SQL error message that reveals query structure
Try basic SQLi payloads like: ' OR '1'='1
Test UNION-based injection: ' UNION SELECT NULL--
Analyze error messages to understand the database structure

idor.what: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) occurs when an application exposes a direct reference to an internal object (like a database key) without proper authorization checks, allowing attackers to access other users' data.
idor.why: Attackers can view, modify, or delete other users' sensitive information simply by changing ID parameters in URLs or requests. This is a broken access control vulnerability.
idor.impact: CVSS 7.5 (High) - OWASP A01: Broken Access Control

hints.title: Beginner Hint
hints.text: Notice the order ID in the URL. What happens if you change it to a different number?

hints.title: Intermediate Hint
hints.text: Try sequential numbers: 1001, 1002, 1003. The application isn't checking if you own these orders!

hints.title: Solution
hints.text: Change the order ID to 1002 or 1003 to access other users' order data. No authentication required!

fix.secure:
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $orderId AND user_id = $currentUserId;
// Always check ownership!

steps: Note the current order ID in the URL parameter
Try changing it to 1001, then 1002, then 1003
Observe that you can access orders from different users
Check the returned data - does it belong to you?
This demonstrates missing authorization checks

localstorage.what: Sensitive data stored in browser localStorage or sessionStorage can be accessed by any JavaScript running on the page, including malicious scripts injected via XSS attacks.
localstorage.why: If authentication tokens, API keys, or personal data are stored in browser storage, XSS attackers can steal them instantly. This data persists even after the user closes the browser.

hints.title: Beginner Hint
hints.text: Click the 'Dump Storage' button to see what's in localStorage and sessionStorage.

hints.title: Intermediate Hint
hints.text: Open Browser DevTools → Application tab → Local Storage to inspect manually.

hints.title: Solution
hints.text: The dump will reveal API keys, tokens, and other sensitive data that should never be client-side.

steps: Click the 'Dump LocalStorage' button
Examine the output for sensitive data
Open DevTools → Application → Local Storage
Note any API keys, tokens, or personal information
Remember: any JavaScript can read this data!

secret-scanner.what: Hardcoded secrets in client-side code (JavaScript, HTML comments, or page source) are exposed to anyone who views the page source. This includes API keys, tokens, passwords, and internal URLs.
secret-scanner.why: Attackers can steal API keys to access paid services on your dime, gain unauthorized access to internal systems, or escalate privileges using exposed credentials.

hints.title: Beginner Hint
hints.text: View the page source (Ctrl+U or Cmd+U) and look for comments or embedded secrets.

hints.title: Intermediate Hint
hints.text: Search for keywords like 'API', 'key', 'secret', 'password', 'token' in the source code.

hints.title: Solution
hints.text: Check HTML comments, JavaScript variables (window.APP_CONFIG), and inline scripts for exposed secrets.

fix.insecure:
const API_KEY = 'sk_live_abc123';
// Secret exposed in client code!

steps: Right-click the page and select 'View Page Source'
Search (Ctrl+F) for: API, key, secret, password, token
Check HTML comments <!-- --> for hidden data
Open DevTools Console and inspect global variables
Look for configuration objects like window.APP_CONFIG

git-exposure.what: Exposed .git directories allow attackers to download the entire source code repository, including commit history, configuration files, and potentially hardcoded credentials.
git-exposure.why: Attackers can reconstruct your entire codebase, find vulnerabilities by reading the source, and extract secrets from commit history even if they've been removed in recent commits.

hints.title: Beginner Hint
hints.text: Try accessing /.git/config or /.git/HEAD in your browser.

hints.title: Intermediate Hint
hints.text: If .git is exposed, you can reconstruct the repository using tools like git-dumper.

hints.title: Solution
hints.text: Navigate to /.git/config to confirm exposure. Real attackers would download the full repo.

fix.insecure:
# .git directory publicly accessible
# Server serves all files
fix.secure:
# In .htaccess or nginx config:
RedirectMatch 404 /\.git
# Or ensure .git is outside web root!

steps: Try accessing /.git/config in your browser
Check if /.git/HEAD returns content
In production, use tools like git-dumper to extract the full repo
Review extracted files for hardcoded secrets
Check git history for removed but still visible secrets

env-file.what: Exposed .env files contain environment variables with database credentials, API keys, and other sensitive configuration that should never be public.
env-file.why: Database passwords, AWS keys, and API tokens in .env files give attackers complete access to your backend systems and third-party services.

hints.title: Beginner Hint
hints.text: Try accessing /.env in your browser URL.

hints.title: Intermediate Hint
hints.text: Look for database credentials, API keys, and secret keys in the .env file.

hints.title: Solution
hints.text: Navigate to /.env and view the exposed credentials. Never deploy .env to production!

fix.insecure:
# .env file in web root
# Accessible via HTTP

steps: Navigate to /.env in the browser
Examine the exposed environment variables
Note database passwords, API keys, JWT secrets
In real scenarios, these could be used to compromise the entire system
Always keep .env files outside the web root!

cors.what: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) misconfiguration occurs when a website allows any origin to make authenticated requests, enabling attackers to steal user data from malicious websites.
cors.why: An attacker can create a malicious website that makes requests to your API on behalf of logged-in users, stealing their data or performing actions without their knowledge.

hints.title: Beginner Hint
hints.text: Check the Network tab in DevTools for 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' headers in the response.

hints.title: Intermediate Hint
hints.text: Look for 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *' combined with 'Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true'.

hints.title: Solution
hints.text: The API allows all origins (*) with credentials - a dangerous combination that enables data theft.

steps: Open DevTools → Network tab
Make a request to the /api/cors endpoint
Inspect the response headers
Look for Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Note the security violation when combined with credentials

upload.what: File upload vulnerabilities occur when applications don't properly validate uploaded files, allowing attackers to upload malicious files (shells, scripts) and execute them on the server.
upload.why: Attackers can gain complete control of the server by uploading and executing malicious code, leading to data breaches, ransomware, or using the server for attacks.

hints.title: Beginner Hint
hints.text: Try uploading a file with a double extension like 'shell.php.jpg'.

hints.title: Intermediate Hint
hints.text: Test MIME type validation by changing the Content-Type header while keeping a dangerous extension.

hints.title: Solution
hints.text: Use double extensions, null bytes (file.php%00.jpg), or path traversal (../../shell.php) to bypass filters.

steps: Try uploading a normal image file first
Then try shell.php.jpg (double extension)
Test file.php%00.jpg (null byte injection)
Try ../../../shell.php (path traversal)
Observe which bypass techniques work

input-validation.what: Input validation vulnerabilities occur when applications don't properly sanitize or validate user input, allowing special characters and encoding to bypass security filters.
input-validation.why: Improper validation enables SQL injection, XSS, path traversal, and other injection attacks. Every input is a potential attack vector.

hints.title: Beginner Hint
hints.text: Try URL encoding special characters: %2e%2e%2f for ../

hints.title: Intermediate Hint
hints.text: Test double encoding, null bytes (%00), and Unicode normalization bypasses.

hints.title: Solution
hints.text: Use payloads like: %2e%2e%2f, ....//,  ..;/, or %00 to bypass basic filters.

steps: Test basic characters that should be blocked
Try URL encoding: %2e for . or %2f for /
Test double encoding: %252e for %2e
Try null byte injection: payload%00.txt
Observe which encoding bypasses work

security-headers.what: Missing security headers leave web applications vulnerable to clickjacking, XSS, and other client-side attacks that proper HTTP headers could prevent.
security-headers.why: Headers like Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, and Strict-Transport-Security provide defense-in-depth against various attack vectors.

hints.title: Beginner Hint
hints.text: Open DevTools → Network tab and check the response headers for security-related headers.

hints.title: Intermediate Hint
hints.text: Look for missing headers: Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Strict-Transport-Security.

hints.title: Solution
hints.text: The application is missing critical security headers, making it vulnerable to XSS, clickjacking, and MITM attacks.

fix.secure:
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'
X-Frame-Options: DENY
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000
Referrer-Policy: no-referrer

steps: Open DevTools → Network tab
Load the page and select the document request
Click on the 'Headers' tab
Check for presence of security headers
Note which critical headers are missing

clickjacking.what: Clickjacking (UI redressing) tricks users into clicking on something different from what they perceive, typically by overlaying an invisible iframe over legitimate UI elements.
clickjacking.why: Attackers can trick users into performing unintended actions like changing account settings, authorizing payments, or granting permissions without their knowledge.

hints.title: Beginner Hint
hints.text: Check if the page can be loaded in an iframe by examining the X-Frame-Options header.

hints.title: Intermediate Hint
hints.text: If X-Frame-Options is missing or set to ALLOW, the page is vulnerable to clickjacking.

hints.title: Solution
hints.text: The missing X-Frame-Options header allows this page to be embedded in iframes on malicious sites.

steps: Check response headers for X-Frame-Options
Try embedding the page in an iframe
Note that it loads successfully (vulnerability confirmed)
Understand how an attacker would overlay invisible elements
Consider impact on sensitive actions (transfers, deletions)
